blocks: Local Council Approves New Cycling Lanes
By Sarah Mitchell · 4 min read
The city council voted 7–2 on Tuesday to approve a network of protected cycling lanes along three of the busiest roads in the downtown area, ending a debate that has lasted more than two years.
Supporters say the lanes will make cycling safer and reduce traffic congestion, while some business owners worry that the loss of parking spaces will drive customers away.
Construction is expected to begin next spring and will be carried out in stages to keep roads open. The first section, on Market Street, should be finished by the end of June.
"This is a big step for everyone who wants to get around the city without a car," said council member David Chen, who first proposed the plan.
Residents can view the full plan and leave comments on the council's website until December 15.

blocks: How Night Trains Made a Comeback in Europe
Ten years ago, many people thought sleeper trains were finished. Rail companies were cutting routes, carriages were old, and cheap flights had made overnight rail travel look slow and expensive.
Today the picture is very different. New routes connect cities such as Vienna, Paris, Amsterdam and Berlin, and many of them sell out weeks in advance during the summer and around holidays.

Part of the reason is climate. A seat on a night train produces far less carbon dioxide than the same trip by plane, and a growing number of travellers say this matters when they choose how to travel.

Convenience also plays a role. A night train leaves from the city centre in the evening and arrives in another city centre the next morning, saving both a hotel night and the time spent getting to and from airports.
Governments have helped too. Several countries now support new connections with public money, and the European Union has named cross-border rail as a priority for the coming decade.

Not everything is solved, however. Tickets can still cost more than a flight, especially for travellers who book late, and delays on one national network can affect a train that crosses three or four borders.

Operators also say they need more modern carriages. Building a sleeper car takes years, and only a few factories in Europe can make them, so new routes are often limited by the number of vehicles available.
Passengers have their own wishes. Many ask for better Wi-Fi, quieter compartments and simpler booking across different companies, which today often requires several websites and separate tickets.
Despite these problems, most experts expect demand to keep growing. If prices fall and more carriages arrive, night trains could become a normal choice for trips of up to about 1,500 kilometres.
For now, travellers who want to try one are advised to book early, bring earplugs and a light snack, and leave a little extra time for connections on the morning of arrival.
